3. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the present appellants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action to file the present suit; the suit is barred by limitation; that the defendant No.1 has been residing in India since 1971; the right of repurchase of the plaintiffs through Ekrarnama is extinguished after expiry of the period mentioned in the Ekrarnama and the transaction was treated as an out and out sale; the contesting defendants have purchased the suit land for valuable consideration bonafide without notice of Ekrarnama and have been possessing the suit land; the price of the suit land is increased meanwhile and, as such, the plaintiffs have filed the present suit on false statement and, as such, they are not entitled to any relief as prayed for and the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 "The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division has failed to notice that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no application to the transaction in question which had been past and closed before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside and that of the trial Court restored." 

 6. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submitted that the High Court Division wrongly relied on the decisions reported in 34 DLR (AD) L37 and 36 DLR 90 which are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The learned Advocate further submitted that the High Court Division failed to take notice that section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has no application to a transaction which was past and closed before the promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972. 

 7. Mr AY Ahmed Ali, the learned Counsel appeared for the respondents though did not file the concise statement but in view of the importance of the point involved we have heard him, who has relied on the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 233 and submitted that admittedly the plaintiffs who were owners of the suit land sold the same by registered kabala dated 5-2-1963 to the defendant No.2 with a condition to re-purchase on payment of the consideration money and on the same day executed an Ekrarnama to return the suit land, within Chaitra 1377 BS making the contract an usufructuary mortgage for which Article 148 of the Limitation Act provided a period of limitation of 60 years to make the suit barred by limitation and he further submits that by operation of section 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after expiry of 7 years, the suit land automatically vests in the plaintiff and the transaction is not past and closed as has been submitted by the learned Counsel. 

 "Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos.88 and 136 of 1972 and No.24 of 1973 are all valid legislations for affecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vires; (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either by way of out and out sale with an agreement to recovery or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question; (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No.88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to recover, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972; and (5) as far as the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions, past and closed." 

 "But on perusal of the judgment of the High Court Division it is found that learned Advocates of both the parties who appeared they were confused between the period of subsistence of a usufructuary mortgage and the period of limitation in the case of a suit for redemption of a mortgaged land. The maximum period for which a usufructuary mortgage can be entered into was fifteen years under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. But by Ordinance No. XXI of 1969, section 95 was amended and thereby the maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgager does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption. In this case the suit was filed just on the accrual of the right of redemption and, as such, it is not barred by limitation. 

 10. The moot question involved in this case has been resolved ultimately in the case of Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat vs Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat and another reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90. The fact of the case was that respondent No.1 therein purchased one acre of land from the appellant by a registered kabala dated 24-6-1967 for a consideration of Taka 2,000 and on the same date executed a registered agreement to recovery the kabala land if the consideration of money was repaid within 4 years from that date. The appellant filed the Miscellaneous Case No. 1227 of 1972-73 in the Court of the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Barisal (South) to get the land redeemed. The suit was dismissed and the appeal was also dismissed. The High Court Division, however, made the rule absolute holding that as the date of reconveyance expired on 1-3-1972 before the President's Order No.88 of 1972 came into force on 3-8-1972 the transaction in question could not, be treated as a usufructuary mortgage transaction in the light of the decision in Bangladesh vs Haji Abdul Gani Biswas reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233 and the appellant was not entitled to get back the case land on the basis of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the transaction was not subsisting one on the date of promulgation of PO No.88 of 1972 as contemplated under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
